# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it carefully and checked the numbers. This report settles several questions the earlier papers left open, and mostly holds its claims at the right weight. I have three main concerns:

1. The summary's comparison of 12.5% with 8.5% mixes two hours measures.
2. The claimed decline is treated as established when it hasn't been tested.
3. A simple time-accounting check suggests meetings may explain more of the gain than the mediation model finds. That would change how the result should be read.

## What it reports

**Varden case-processing offices (7 v 7) at 24 months**

- **Output per FTE:** −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2).
- **Hours:** −12% on timesheets and −11% on a new system-log measure.
- **Output per hour:** +9.8% on timesheets (down from 12.5% at nine months) and +8.5% on logs (3.4 to 13.8).
- **Quality and staffing:** appeal overturns are unchanged. Sick days fell 27% and resignations were lower.

**Registered mediation**

- **Recurring meetings** fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours a week in treated offices and from 7.2 to 7.0 in control offices. They explain 47% of the gain.
- **Fatigue** explains 18%, and 35% is unexplained.

**Two control offices that ran a "meeting audit"** cut meeting time by 2.1 hours and gained 4.1% per hour against their own past. The authors say plainly that this is suggestive only, and that the trial can't tell whether reorganisation alone would capture the gain.

**Counter arm.** The county ended it at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices. Restoring service would need 12% more staff, at about 9% more per contact.

**Halden subset.** Of the 14 organisations that responded, 3 reverted: hospitality, retail and a marketing agency, with output of 88–91 at reversion. The 11 that continued show output at 96.8 and hours down 13.4%, giving +11.8% per hour. The authors frame this as an upper bound for organisations that self-selected into the change.

**On the earlier papers.** The report says the gain survives the re-analysis's own standards, so "entirely an artifact" is refuted. It also reports that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they can't speak to decay.

## Arithmetic

- **Per-hour gains:** 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% and 0.966/0.89 = +8.5%.
- **Log-based CI:** reproduces from the per-FTE interval.
- **Halden subset:** 34.9/40.3 = −13.4% and 96.8/86.6 = +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Meeting change:** −3.5 against −0.2 hours, a difference of 3.3 hours. This matches the cross-sectional gap at nine months.
- **County costing:** 12% more staff restores contacts (1/0.886 ≈ 1.13). With staff costs around three-quarters of total cost, the result is about 9% more per contact. That staff-cost share is my assumption, not the report's.

## What this settles, and should be held at full weight

- **"Entirely an artifact" is refuted, at least in this setting.** A randomised, registered estimate with record-based output and log-measured hours, at two years, gives +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). It meets every standard the re-analysis set.
- **Timesheet understatement is small:** about one percentage point. Measured hours are no longer a meaningful source of doubt in Varden.
- **The meeting gap was not pre-existing.** I raised this concern before. The baselines were 7.4 and 7.2 hours, so the gap opened during the trial.
- **The meta-analysis's long-run evidence can't address decay.** I suspected the four studies were uncontrolled or used scheduled hours. They were both, so its conclusion that novelty "can be set aside" has nothing behind it.
- **Coverage-bound work is now closed.** The employer ended the arm on service grounds.
- **The Halden subset is framed correctly.** Calling it "survivors twice over" and an upper bound is the right weight.

## Points to address

**1. The summary compares across measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is on timesheets and the 8.5% on logs. The like-for-like change is 12.5% to 9.8%, a decline of about a fifth, not the third the summary implies. Section 5's "about a quarter" falls between the two.

**2. The decline is a point estimate, not an established finding.** The intervals at nine and 24 months (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily, and no confidence interval is given for the change. Section 3's wording, "consistent with some fading," is right. Section 5 states the decline as fact, which repeats in milder form the error the report correctly identifies in the meta-analysis.

**3. Simple time accounting suggests meetings may explain nearly all of the per-hour gain.** These are my rough calculations from the reported figures:

| Treated offices | Baseline | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Hours | 37.9 | about 33.4 (−12%) |
| Meetings | 7.4 | 3.9 |
| Non-meeting time | about 30.5 | about 29.5 (about −3.4%) |

Control offices' non-meeting time rose slightly. So relative to control, non-meeting time fell about 4%, and output per FTE fell 3.4%. **Output per non-meeting hour is then essentially unchanged (about +1%).** On this accounting, staff didn't work faster. They spent less of a shorter week in meetings, and output followed the time spent on cases.

This assumes meetings produce no counted output, and that log hours include meeting time; see point 4. If the assumptions hold, the mediation model's 47% for meetings looks low and its 18% for fatigue looks high. The difference may come from the model's specification. It deserves a direct check, because it changes the policy reading from "rested workers are more productive" to "a shorter week forced out low-value time." The two control offices fit this reading roughly. Cutting 2.1 meeting hours at constant hours would predict about +7% under this accounting, and they found +4.1%.

**4. What exactly do the system logs measure?** They are described as recording "time staff are working on cases." If that is literal, meetings wouldn't appear in log hours, and logs should show hours falling by only about 4%, not 11%. The reported −11% suggests logs capture total logged-in time. The definition matters for interpreting the mediation results and the accounting in point 3.

**5. The mediation is registered, but uses the same offices.** The hypothesis came from month-six variation across these same seven treated offices. The test is genuinely prospective in time, but not an independent sample: offices that cut meetings early may differ in persistent ways. "Survives a registered test" is fair. "Confirms," in the summary, is a step further. Two further caveats apply:

- **Few clusters.** There are 14 offices, so the mediation CIs may be too narrow without a small-cluster correction.
- **The pathways may overlap.** Fewer meetings could itself reduce fatigue, so the two shares may not be separable.

**6. The Halden hours baseline looks borrowed.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the figure for all 27 time-tracking organisations in the re-analysis. The 11 continuing organisations need their own baseline. Nine of the 23 also didn't respond, so the respondents are self-selected a third time.

**7. The marketing agency reverted for a different reason.** It is "discretionary" work by the meta-analysis's coding, yet it reverted over *client deadlines*. Externally timed demand may be a third category, distinct from both backlog work and coverage.

**8. Items from the nine-month report still not addressed:**

- CIs for the quality measures
- backlog and time-to-decision data
- sick days per *scheduled* day, which matters because fewer scheduled days mechanically means fewer sick days

## Where the evidence stands now

**Found**

- **Discretionary, backlog-type public work:** a per-hour gain of about 8.5–10% persists to 24 months, with output per worker slightly below control.
- **Coverage-bound work:** output falls and service worsens, and the arm was abandoned.
- **Headline figures above 20%:** mostly artifacts of design and measurement.
- **Timesheets:** understate hours only slightly.

**Open**

- **Whether the gain declined between nine and 24 months:** the point estimate fell, but the change is untested.
- **Durability beyond 24 months, and results in private-sector knowledge work.**
- **How much of the gain is reallocation away from meetings rather than faster work:** my accounting suggests most of it.
- **The decisive question, as the report itself says:** can reorganisation without an hours cut capture the gain, or is the cut what makes reorganisation happen and stick? Answering it needs a three-arm trial: hours cut, meeting audit only, and control.

I can work the time-accounting check up properly as a note to the authors, or extend the evidence brief to include this report.
